stories.headline: Thornton Youth Pastor Sentenced to 13 Years to Life for Child Sex Assault
stories.summary:
Joshua Lucero, 29, a youth pastor at Word Alive Church in Thornton, was sentenced Friday to 13 years to life in the Colorado Department of Corrections after an Adams County jury convicted him in May of sexual assault on a child by one in a position of trust — pattern of abuse. Prosecutors said Lucero developed a secret relationship with a teenage girl in the church's youth group and began sexually assaulting her when she was 16, with incidents occurring an unknown number of times over several years.

Lucero worked at the church where his father was lead pastor, and he led youth events and supervised overnight retreats. When the victim and her parents reported the abuse to church leadership in 2021, leadership chose not to notify law enforcement and attempted to handle the matter internally — prompting three board members to resign and later report the assaults to Thornton Police.

The victim was initially unprepared to press charges but returned to investigators in 2024. Lucero was arrested in March 2025. District Attorney Brian Mason praised the victim's courage in coming forward. Lucero's attorney said he intends to pursue all avenues on appeal.

stories.headline: Ursa Major Opens Longmont Facility Expected to Add 1,850 Aerospace Jobs in Colorado
stories.summary:
Rocket and aerospace manufacturing company Ursa Major opened a new facility in Longmont last week that will produce avionics and in-space propulsion systems. The expansion is projected to create up to 1,850 jobs over the next eight years and secured $35 million in job growth tax incentives and $23 million in CHIPS refundable tax credits from the Colorado Economic Development Commission.

The Berthoud-based company, founded in 2015, currently employs more than 300 workers in Colorado. Officials said the company also considered expanding to Ohio, Mississippi, or California before choosing to remain in its home state. Gov. Jared Polis credited Colorado's aerospace ecosystem — anchored by its central location, high elevation, universities, and military bases — for retaining the expansion.

The announcement comes as Colorado works to maintain its standing as one of the nation's largest aerospace hubs. CEO Chris Spagnoletti said the company is grateful for the state's partnership as it scales up operations.

stories.headline: Downtown Denver 17-Story Office Tower Sells for $3.6 Million After Foreclosure Auction
stories.summary:
A 17-story office tower in downtown Denver sold for $3.63 million following a foreclosure auction, according to the Denver Business Journal. Malik Kuforiji's Adio Palace LLC purchased the property, identified as Columbine Place.

The sale price underscores the continued distress in Denver's downtown office market, where elevated vacancy rates and reduced demand for commercial space have weighed on property values in recent years. The transaction reflects broader challenges facing urban office buildings across the country as hybrid and remote work patterns persist.

The sale adds to a series of discounted downtown Denver real estate transactions that have drawn attention to the city's ongoing efforts to revitalize its central business district.

stories.headline: Denver Public Schools Welcomes Nearly 89,000 Students for First Day of School
stories.summary:
Denver Public Schools kicked off the 2026-27 school year Monday with approximately 89,000 students returning to class across 198 schools — 210 fewer pupils than the prior year. The district's enrollment has declined steadily since a 2019 peak of 92,112 students, a trend Superintendent Alex Marrero attributed to declining birth rates and the rising cost of living in Denver.

Marrero said the district may begin recruiting students from neighboring districts such as Aurora, Adams, and Arapahoe counties in an effort to stabilize enrollment. Despite the enrollment dip, district officials pointed to recent standardized test scores as a bright spot: DPS essentially matched its pre-pandemic English performance and surpassed its pre-pandemic math scores on the 2026 Colorado Measures of Academic Success.

Colorado Department of Education Commissioner Susanna Córdova and DPS Board of Education President Xóchitl Gaytán joined Marrero at Newlon Elementary School on Monday to welcome students and families. The event drew a mix of eager returning students and nervous first-timers, with parents expressing hopes for hands-on learning and strong school-family communication.

stories.headline: Colorado National Parks Offer Free Entry Tuesday for National Park Service's 110th Anniversary
stories.summary:
All of Colorado's national parks and monuments overseen by the National Park Service will offer free admission Tuesday, August 26, in celebration of the agency's 110th anniversary. The NPS was established on August 25, 1916, with a mission to preserve natural and cultural resources for current and future generations.

Colorado's four national parks — Rocky Mountain, Mesa Verde, Great Sand Dunes, and Black Canyon of the Gunnison — along with 13 national monuments, trails, and historic sites will waive entry fees. Visitors to Rocky Mountain National Park will still need a timed entry reservation despite the fee waiver.

Additional free entry days are planned for September 17 (Constitution Day), October 27 (Theodore Roosevelt's birthday), and November 11 (Veterans Day). The free day is part of a broader National Park Week running through Sunday, with themed daily events including Watch Wildlife Wednesday and Freedom Friday.

stories.headline: Colorado Wildfires Grow to 228,000 Acres as Rain Aids Containment Efforts
stories.summary:
Approximately 21 ongoing wildfires are burning roughly 228,000 acres across Colorado, according to CPR News's live wildfire tracker updated through Monday. Recent rainfall and higher humidity have helped firefighters increase containment lines, though agencies say they remain vigilant given the scope of active fire activity.

The fires have continued to stress communities across the state following one of the more destructive wildfire seasons in recent Colorado history. Colorado Parks and Wildlife has also noted that drought conditions tied to the fires have pushed bears into more populated areas in search of food, contributing to a record number of bear-human conflict reports this year.

Residents are encouraged to monitor the CPR News wildfire tracker, which is updated hourly using data from multiple incident and intelligence sources, for the latest information on active fires and smoke conditions.

stories.headline: Near-Total Lunar Eclipse Visible from Colorado on Thursday Night
stories.summary:
A near-total lunar eclipse will be visible from Colorado on Thursday night, offering residents across the metro area and mountains a potential celestial viewing opportunity. Early forecasts suggest relatively dry conditions for much of the state, though meteorologists caution that thunderstorms remain possible, particularly across southeastern Colorado.

For the Denver metro area, early indications point to decent viewing conditions, though forecasters advise residents to check the latest weather outlook before heading out as conditions could shift before Thursday evening. No special equipment is needed to view a lunar eclipse.

The event has generated interest from stargazers across the Front Range ahead of what could be one of the more notable astronomical events visible from Colorado this year.

stories.headline: Fat Marmot Week Launches Monday with Bracket Competition Featuring Colorado's Chunkiest Rodents
stories.summary:
Researchers with the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory's Marmot Project launched Fat Marmot Week on Monday, a bracket-style competition modeled after the popular Fat Bear Week that celebrates the yellow-bellied marmots of Colorado. Eight contenders are competing across rounds on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, with the winner announced Saturday at sites.google.com/view/fatmarmotweek.

The event follows the viral success of the project's OnlyMarms fundraising page, a tongue-in-cheek campaign hosted on OnlyFans that offers G-rated footage of marmots in exchange for tips. The page has raised $6,700 to support research amid federal grant cuts, according to researcher Katie Adler, a UCLA Ph.D. candidate.

Denver Beer Co. is partnering with the event by releasing a limited OnlyMarms Extra Thicc Double IPA, with $1 from every pint and crowler sold donated to the Marmot Project. The competition also includes a separate category for which marmot gained the most body mass over the summer grazing season.

stories.headline: Pat Surtain II Ranked No. 10 on NFL's Top 100 Players List
stories.summary:
Denver Broncos cornerback Pat Surtain II was named the 10th-best player in the NFL on the league's annual top-100 countdown, released Monday. The recognition continues a pattern for the Pro Bowl cornerback, who also checked in at No. 10 on the preseason list a year ago.

Surtain has accumulated an extensive list of accolades in his five NFL seasons, including Defensive Player of the Year honors in 2024, first-team All-Pro selections in 2022 and 2024, and four consecutive Pro Bowl nods. New England offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels, the former Broncos head coach, was shown on video telling Surtain after the Patriots' AFC Championship win over Denver that he is "the best one in the league."

Broncos teammate and defensive lineman Zach Allen, who ranked No. 73 on the same list, credited Surtain's presence with making every other defender's job easier. Surtain said he takes particular pride in deterring opposing offenses from throwing to his side of the field, even when that impact doesn't show up in traditional statistics.

stories.headline: Broncos' Riley Moss Rib Injury 'Nothing Serious,' Payton Says; Wattenberg, Mims Return to Practice
stories.summary:
Denver Broncos head coach Sean Payton said Monday that cornerback Riley Moss, who left Friday's preseason game against Green Bay after the second play with a rib injury, is not seriously hurt. Moss did not practice Monday but was doing light conditioning work on the side field, and Payton said the team will monitor his progress through the week.

The Broncos also received positive injury news on other fronts: center Luke Wattenberg and wide receiver Marvin Mims Jr. both participated in team drills for the first time since sustaining injuries early in training camp, with Wattenberg handling most first-team snaps. Tight end Caleb Lohner, out since late July, was also seen working out on the side field for the first time.

Payton confirmed the team signed veteran safety Taylor Rapp to a one-year, $1.3 million deal — describing the move as one of opportunity rather than necessity. Outside linebacker Drew Sanders, center Alex Forsyth, and Lohner did not practice Monday. The Broncos face an NFL roster cutdown deadline of August 30.

stories.headline: Nuggets' Christian Braun Pushes Back on Critics After DeRozan Signing, Watson Trade
stories.summary:
Denver Nuggets guard Christian Braun dismissed skeptics who have questioned the team's offseason moves, saying the club has "everything we need" heading into the 2026-27 season. Speaking at his youth camp in Lakewood over the weekend, Braun said being written off motivates him and the team, pointing to the franchise's championship pedigree and the continued presence of Nikola Jokic, Jamal Murray, and Aaron Gordon.

The Nuggets have drawn criticism for trading Peyton Watson to Cleveland and signing veteran DeMar DeRozan to a minimum contract while pushing further into the NBA salary cap's second apron. The roster overhaul also saw Tim Hardaway Jr., Jonas Valanciunas, and Jalen Pickett depart, replaced by Marvin Bagley III, Lonnie Walker IV, and DeRozan.

Braun expressed confidence in the front office and said he is excited to play alongside DeRozan, a six-time All-Star. Analysts have noted, however, that the Western Conference has grown more competitive, with Oklahoma City still loaded and San Antonio's Victor Wembanyama entering his prime, raising questions about the Nuggets' championship window.

stories.headline: Park Hill Cat Tour Returns Sunday with More Than 200 Registered Participants
stories.summary:
The third annual Park Hill Cat Tour, a free walking tour of the northeast Denver neighborhood celebrating local felines, takes place Sunday with more than 200 registered participants — enough to force organizer Megan Nyce to close RSVPs over concerns about traffic and crowd management. The event allows registered attendees to stroll through Park Hill stopping at homes where residents showcase their cats from front lawns and window perches.

Nyce, inspired by similar cat tours in Minneapolis, said the event has grown rapidly since its debut and has become one of the most anticipated community gatherings in the neighborhood. This year she recruited a second tour guide, David Obuchowski, father of Captain Calvin Marshmallow, a rescued Norwegian Forest Cat who appeared on last year's tour.

Residents wishing to feature their cats can still sign up to participate as hosts at parkhillcattour.com. Organizers say the event reflects a community appetite for lighthearted, neighborly gatherings.

topStory.headline: Supreme Court Lifts Injunction on Trump Mail-Ballot Order in 6-3 Ruling Along Ideological Lines
topStory.summary:
The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 6-3 Monday to lift a lower court injunction that had blocked key provisions of President Donald Trump's executive order on mail-in voting, allowing the administration to move forward with portions of the order while litigation continues. The conservative majority sided with the administration in an unsigned per curiam opinion, clearing the way for the Department of Homeland Security to compile a federal citizenship list and share it with states, authorizing the Attorney General to prioritize prosecution of state officials who issue ballots to ineligible voters, and permitting the U.S. Postal Service to proceed with rulemaking on mail ballot design standards.

The ruling does not address what legal experts describe as the most contentious element of the order — a requirement that the Postal Service verify the voting eligibility of each mail ballot recipient and withhold ballots from anyone not appearing on a government list — which remains blocked under a separate nationwide injunction. The court's majority wrote that the Democratic-led plaintiff states had not yet suffered concrete harm from the order and that the Massachusetts district judge who issued the injunction had acted prematurely, adding that the decision 'does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the Order will necessarily be lawful.' The three liberal justices dissented, with Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson writing that the ruling 'needlessly injects chaos and uncertainty into the upcoming midterm elections,' while Justice Sonia Sotomayor, joined by Justice Elena Kagan, argued the dispute should be addressed immediately on its merits.

Trump signed the executive order in March, directing federal agencies to create a 'state citizenship list' of eligible voters and instructing the Postal Service to deliver mail ballots only to individuals on that list. Democratic officials in 23 states and the District of Columbia challenged the order in court, arguing that the U.S. Constitution grants authority over election administration to states and Congress, not the president. U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani of Massachusetts sided with the plaintiff states, ruling that Trump lacked authority to dictate how states run federal elections and questioning whether federal agencies could compile accurate citizenship rolls; an appeals court upheld her ruling before she later issued a second injunction with nationwide effect.

The USPS on Friday published a finalized rule requiring states to collect and report basic voter information attached to a unique barcode on every mail-in ballot, a change the Postal Service said would take effect immediately upon the Supreme Court lifting the injunction. The immediate practical impact on November's midterm elections remains uncertain, with many legal experts saying the ruling alone is unlikely to produce significant changes for voters in the short term. California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced his state would file a new legal challenge, and New York Attorney General Letitia James called the ruling 'a painful setback' while pledging it would not be the final word, signaling that court battles over the order are expected to continue through the election cycle.
